Saudi Arabia.polity: Independent Arabian tribes and towns (Quraysh of Mecca; Aws, Khazraj and Jewish clans of Yathrib); Muslim community at Medina from 622
Saudi Arabia.summary: The Hijaz had no state. Mecca, home of the Quraysh tribe, was a pilgrimage sanctuary around the Kaaba and a trading town on the caravan route; Yathrib (Medina) was an oasis of Arab and Jewish clans. Muhammad ﷺ, born in Mecca, received his first revelation about 610, emigrated to Medina in 622, entered Mecca in 630, and by his death in 632 had united Arabia under Islam.

events.t: Muhammad ﷺ is born in Mecca (c. 570), in the year that, according to tradition, Abraha of South Arabia tried to conquer Mecca.
Muhammad ﷺ receives the first revelation in a cave on Mount Hira near Mecca, at about the age of forty.
The Hijra: Muhammad ﷺ and his followers emigrate from Mecca to Yathrib (Medina); it marks the beginning of the Muslim calendar.
In 2 AH the Muslims of Medina win a surprising victory over a Meccan force at Badr.
In 8 AH Muhammad ﷺ enters Mecca with 10,000 men; the city submits, and he dedicates it to God as the centre of Muslim pilgrimage.
Muhammad ﷺ dies in Medina (11 AH); Abu Bakr becomes caliph and faces the tribal uprisings known as the Ridda.

Saudi Arabia.link: This was the homeland of Muhammad ﷺ and of the first Muslim community, at Mecca and Medina.

sources.title: Islamic world: the emigration of Muhammad ﷺ to Yathrib (Medina)
Ibn Ishaq, The Life of Muhammad ﷺ (Sirat Rasul Allah, recension of Ibn Hisham), trans. A. Guillaume, 1955
Safiur-Rahman Mubarakpuri, Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum (The Sealed Nectar)

Yemen.polity: Former Himyarite kingdom under Ethiopian (Aksumite) rule, then a Sasanian Persian dependency from c. 570
Yemen.summary: After Ethiopia intervened in 525, south Arabia became an Ethiopian protectorate under Abraha and his son Masruq. About 570 a Persian force under Vahriz, backing Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan, killed Masruq and took Sanaa. Persian governors then ruled, and the descendants of Persian soldiers and Arab mothers were called the Abna. The last governor, Badhan, accepted Islam, recorded under 10 AH (631).

events.t: According to Islamic tradition, Abraha of South Arabia tries to conquer Mecca in the year Muhammad ﷺ is born.
A Persian force under Vahriz defeats and kills Abraha's son Masruq, ending Ethiopian rule (c. 570; some sources date Masruq's death to 575–576 or 582).
Badhan, Persian governor of Yemen, and other Abna leaders accept Islam, recorded under 10 AH (631).
A Yemeni rising led by al-Aswad, who claimed prophetic powers, expels agents of Muhammad ﷺ (March 632); al-Aswad is later killed.

Yemen.link: Yemen's Persian governor Badhan and other Abna leaders accepted Islam in the lifetime of Muhammad ﷺ, who confirmed the governor as his agent in Yemen.

sources.title: Arabia ii. The Sasanians and Arabia
ʿArab ii. Arab conquest of Iran
Ibn Ishaq, The Life of Muhammad ﷺ (Sirat Rasul Allah, recension of Ibn Hisham), trans. A. Guillaume, 1955

Oman.polity: Azd and other Arab tribes under the Julanda family, Sasanian vassals; the coast part of the Sasanian province of Mazun
Oman.summary: A treaty under Khosrow I gave the Julanda family paramountcy over the Arabs of Oman as tributaries and auxiliaries of Persia, while Persian officials and garrisons held the coast, part of the province of Mazun, and Rustaq inland. After Mecca submitted in 630, the rulers of Oman accepted Islam through Amr ibn al-As, sent by Muhammad ﷺ.

events.t: The Julanda rulers lead Oman's Arabs as Sasanian vassals, while the coast forms part of the Sasanian province of Mazun.
The rulers of Oman accept Islam after Amr ibn al-As arrives as envoy of Muhammad ﷺ.

Oman.link: The rulers of Oman accepted Islam c. 630 through Amr ibn al-As, envoy of Muhammad ﷺ.

sources.title: ʿArab i. Arabs and Iran in the pre-Islamic period
Arabia ii. The Sasanians and Arabia
ʿArab ii. Arab conquest of Iran

United Arab Emirates.polity: Arab tribes of the wider Oman region, within the Sasanian sphere
United Arab Emirates.summary: This coast belonged to the wider Oman region, where the Julanda family held paramountcy over the Arabs as tributaries of Persia, and Persian garrisons, including one at the tip of the Musandam peninsula, guarded the entrance to the Gulf.

events.t: The rulers of Oman accept Islam through Amr ibn al-As, envoy of Muhammad ﷺ; Persia's Arab protégés in Oman also recognize him.

United Arab Emirates.link: As part of the Oman region, its tribes came under the Julanda rulers, who accepted Islam c. 630.

sources.title: ʿArab i. Arabs and Iran in the pre-Islamic period
ʿArab ii. Arab conquest of Iran

Qatar.polity: Arab communities of eastern Arabia (Bahrain region) within the Sasanian sphere
Qatar.summary: Qatar lay in eastern Arabia, then called Bahrain (the northeastern Arabian mainland), where Sasanian Persia ruled through Arab allies and a Persian governor (marzban) at Hajar. After Mecca fell to Muhammad ﷺ in 630, the marzban at Hajar converted to Islam and recognized him, as did Persia's Arab protégés in Bahrain.

events.t: Eastern Arabia, including this peninsula, lies within the Sasanian sphere, with a Persian governor at Hajar.
The Persian governor at Hajar converts to Islam and recognizes Muhammad ﷺ.

Qatar.link: Eastern Arabia's Persian governor at Hajar converted to Islam and recognized Muhammad ﷺ c. 630.

sources.title: ʿArab ii. Arab conquest of Iran
Arabia ii. The Sasanians and Arabia

Kuwait.polity: Arab tribes on the Sasanian frontier of southern Mesopotamia
Kuwait.summary: The Kuwait coast lay at the southern edge of Sasanian Mesopotamia, between eastern Arabia and the port of Ubulla. Bedouin tribes such as the Bakr ibn Wa'il ranged along this frontier, and their victory over the Persians at Dhu Qar, sometime between 604 and 613, showed the weakness of Persian defences.

events.t: Khalid ibn al-Walid defeats the Sasanian frontier commander Hormoz at Dhat al-Salasil, between Bahrain and Ubulla, opening the Muslim campaign in Iraq.

sources.title: ʿArab i. Arabs and Iran in the pre-Islamic period
ʿArab ii. Arab conquest of Iran

Iraq.polity: Sasanian Empire (capital Ctesiphon), with the Lakhmid Arab client kingdom at al-Hira until 602; Kurdish tribes in the northern mountains
Iraq.summary: Mesopotamia, with the capital Ctesiphon, was the most important part of the Sasanian Empire. Khosrow II ended the Lakhmid kingdom of al-Hira in 602, weakening the desert frontier. In the northern mountains, the edge of the Zagros, lived Kurdish tribes who herded sheep and goats. By the end of the Sasanian period the Kurds were a major people of the Zagros; the name Kurd is securely attested from the 7th century, when they converted to Islam.

events.t: Khosrow II deposes and kills al-Nu'man III, ending the Lakhmid kingdom of al-Hira.
Arab tribes led by the Bakr ibn Wa'il defeat a Persian force at Dhu Qar near Kufa; the date is disputed, c. 604–613.
Heraclius defeats the Persian army near Nineveh on 12 December and advances toward Ctesiphon.
Khosrow II is overthrown and executed; his son Kavad II makes peace with Byzantium and dies later that year.
Arab Muslim armies win at al-Qadisiyya and take Ctesiphon (dates disputed, c. 636–637).

Iraq.link: The end of the Lakhmids and the Arab victory at Dhu Qar weakened Persia's Arabian frontier, which Muslim armies crossed in 633.

sources.title: ʿArab i. Arabs and Iran in the pre-Islamic period
ʿArab ii. Arab conquest of Iran
Egypt iv. Relations in the Sasanian period
Iran v. Peoples of Iran (2): Pre-Islamic (C. J. Brunner)

Iran.polity: Sasanian Empire (Hormizd IV, Khosrow II, then rapid succession); Kurdish tribes in the Zagros mountains
Iran.summary: Iran was the core of the Sasanian Empire, whose state religion was Zoroastrianism, with great fire temples such as Adur Gushnasp. Khosrow II conquered vast Byzantine lands after 603 but lost the war in 622–628 and was killed in 628; Yazdegerd III took the throne in 632. In the Zagros the Kurds were by the end of the Sasanian period a major people, herding sheep and goats; they later fought against the Arab invaders.

events.t: The general Bahram Chobin rebels and Hormizd IV is deposed and killed; Khosrow II flees to Byzantine territory.
With help from the Byzantine emperor Maurice, Khosrow II defeats Bahram Chobin and regains the throne.
Heraclius invades Atropatene and sacks the fire temple of Adur Gushnasp near Ganzak (623 or 624, date disputed).
Khosrow II is deposed and executed; his son Kavad II makes peace with Byzantium.
Yazdegerd III, the last Sasanian king, comes to the throne after years of turmoil.

Iran.link: Abandoned after the fall of Khosrow II, Persian governors in Yemen and Bahrain became Muslims and recognized Muhammad ﷺ (c. 628–632).

sources.title: Armenia and Iran ii. The pre-Islamic period
ʿArab ii. Arab conquest of Iran
Iran v. Peoples of Iran (2): Pre-Islamic (C. J. Brunner)

Syria.polity: Byzantine Empire, with Ghassanid Arab allies; Persian occupation c. 611–628
Syria.summary: Syria was a rich Byzantine land of cities such as Antioch and Damascus, with Ghassanid Arab allies guarding the desert side; Meccan merchants traded here. Persian armies took Antioch about 610–612 and occupied Syria after defeating Heraclius in 613, holding it until Kavad II returned Persia's conquests in 628.

events.t: Persian armies under Shahrbaraz take Antioch (date disputed, 610–612).
The Persians defeat a Byzantine army under Heraclius and occupy Syria, including Damascus.
Kavad II returns his father's conquests, and Byzantine rule over Syria is restored.
Antioch falls to the Arab Muslim armies (637–638).

Syria.link: Meccan caravans traded in Syria; tradition says the young Muhammad ﷺ, travelling there with his uncle, was recognized as a future prophet by a Christian monk.

Lebanon.polity: Byzantine Empire, under Persian occupation c. 612–628
Lebanon.summary: The Lebanese coast was part of Byzantine Syria. During the great war Persian armies captured Antioch and pushed through to the Mediterranean coast in 612, then occupied Syria; Byzantium regained the region when Kavad II returned Persia's conquests under the peace of 628.

events.t: Persian armies take Antioch and push on to the Mediterranean coast during their conquest of Syria.
Under the peace of 628, Persia gives up its conquests and Byzantine authority returns.

Israel.summary: This land was part of Byzantine Palestine, with Christian and Jewish communities. When Persia took Jerusalem in 614, Jews were allowed to settle in the city, but this was reversed within two years under Christian pressure. Persia placed Palestine, with its desert frontage, under direct rule in 616 and gave up its conquests under the peace of 628.

events.t: Persian forces under Shahrbaraz conquer Palestine and capture Jerusalem.
Persia places Palestine under direct rule, having reversed its permission for Jews to settle in Jerusalem.
Persia gives up its conquests under the peace of 628, and Byzantine rule returns.

Palestine.summary: Jerusalem was a great Byzantine Christian city. In 614 Persian forces captured it and carried the True Cross to Ctesiphon, a shock to the Christian world. Heraclius triumphantly restored the Cross to Jerusalem in 630, a few years before the Arab conquest of Palestine (634–640).

events.t: Persian forces take Jerusalem and carry the True Cross to Ctesiphon.
In Medina, the Muslim direction of prayer changes from Jerusalem to the Kaaba in Mecca, eighteen months after the Hijra, according to tradition.
Heraclius triumphantly restores the True Cross to Jerusalem.

Palestine.link: Jerusalem was the first direction of prayer of the early Muslims, until a revelation about eighteen months after the Hijra turned them toward the Kaaba.

Jordan.polity: Byzantine Empire, with Ghassanid Arab allies; Persian occupation c. 614–628
Jordan.summary: This land lay in Byzantine provinces whose desert edge was guarded by Arab allies, chiefly the Ghassanids, who protected the spice route from southern Arabia. Persia held the region during the great war. In 630 Muhammad ﷺ campaigned to the Syrian border at Tabuk, where various towns submitted to him, and in 636 the Byzantine defeat at the Yarmuk River opened the region to the Muslims.

events.t: Persia establishes direct rule over Palestine, including its desert frontage.
Muhammad ﷺ leads a campaign to the Syrian border at Tabuk and secures the submission of various towns.
Arab Muslim forces defeat a Byzantine army at the Yarmuk River, opening Palestine and Syria to Muslim control.

Jordan.link: In 630 Muhammad ﷺ led a campaign to Tabuk on the Syrian frontier, where various towns submitted to him.

Turkey.summary: Anatolia and Constantinople formed the heart of the Byzantine Empire, ruled by Maurice, then the usurper Phocas, then Heraclius from 610. Persian armies conquered Asia Minor and reached Chalcedon, across from the capital. In 626 Constantinople survived an Avar siege while a Persian army waited across the Bosporus. The Kurds, today a large population in the southeast, are documented in this period mainly in the Zagros mountains to the east, in what are now Iran and Iraq.

events.t: An army mutiny brings Phocas to power and the emperor Maurice is executed, giving Khosrow II a pretext for war.
Heraclius overthrows Phocas and becomes emperor.
A Persian army under Shahin enters Chalcedon and camps within sight of Constantinople.
Heraclius begins annual campaigns against Persia.
Constantinople withstands a siege by the Avars while a Persian army waits on the Asian shore.

sources.title: Iran v. Peoples of Iran (2): Pre-Islamic (C. J. Brunner)

Cyprus.polity: Byzantine Empire; autocephalous (self-governing) Church of Cyprus
Cyprus.summary: Cyprus was a Byzantine island whose church had been independent of Antioch since 488. A 6th-century mosaic at Kiti shows close artistic ties to Constantinople. John the Almsgiver, born at Amathus, became Chalcedonian patriarch of Alexandria and died back on Cyprus. Arab raids came later in the 7th century, and in 688 a treaty neutralized the island.

events.t: John the Almsgiver of Amathus becomes Chalcedonian patriarch of Alexandria (610; some sources say 606), famed for his charity.
With the Persians occupying Alexandria, John flees to his native Cyprus and dies there (619/20; some sources give 616).

sources.title: John Eleemon (from The Oxford Dictionary of Byzantium)

N. Cyprus.summary: The north shared in the life of Byzantine Cyprus and its self-governing church. Its best-known treasure from this period is a set of nine silver plates showing the life of David, made in Constantinople under Emperor Heraclius (stamps dated 613–629/30). They were found together in 1902 in the Kyrenia district and are now divided between the Metropolitan Museum and the Cyprus Museum in Nicosia.

events.t: Silver plates showing David's life are made in Constantinople (c. 629–630), possibly commemorating an event of Heraclius's reign; they were later found in northern Cyprus.

sources.title: Plate with the Presentation of David to Saul
Steven H. Wander, 'The Cyprus Plates: The Story of David and Goliath', Metropolitan Museum Journal 8, 1973

Armenia.polity: Divided between the Byzantine Empire and Sasanian Persia (Persarmenia); Armenian noble houses
Armenia.summary: Armenia was ruled by noble families such as the Bagratunis and Mamikonians under two empires. In 591 Khosrow II ceded western Persian Armenia to Byzantium, but Persia recovered it after 603. A council at Dvin in 596 rejected Chalcedon. Heraclius campaigned through Armenia from 623, and his victories enabled him to insist on the frontier of 591.

events.t: Khosrow II cedes western Persian Armenia, up to the river Azat, to Byzantium in return for help in regaining his throne.
A church council at Dvin, sponsored by Sembat Bagratuni, rejects the doctrines of the Council of Chalcedon.
Persian forces take Karin (modern Erzurum) as they reconquer Byzantine Armenia (607–608).
Heraclius campaigns through Armenia into Atropatene against Persian forces (623–624).
After Heraclius's victories, Persia consents to restore the Armenian frontier fixed in 591.

sources.title: Armenia and Iran ii. The pre-Islamic period

Azerbaijan.polity: Caucasian Albania (Aghvank) under Sasanian rule, with the Mihrakan princes
Azerbaijan.summary: This land was Caucasian Albania, a Christian land under Persian rule with its capital at Partaw (Barda); it is distinct from Atropatene (Iranian Azerbaijan) to the south. Darband and Partaw were key Persian strongholds against northern raiders. Heraclius wintered here in 624, and Turkic allies of Byzantium, called Khazars in the sources, invaded in 626–628. Varaz Grigor of the Mihrakan family then became prince.

events.t: Heraclius winters his army in Caucasian Albania after striking into Persian Atropatene.
Khazar allies of Heraclius break through the Darband pass, and the Persian governor of Albania flees.
A second Khazar invasion: their leader declares himself lord of Albania.
Varaz Grigor of the Mihrakan family is consecrated prince of Albania (c. 629–630).

Georgia.polity: Kartli (Iberia) under its nobility and client rulers, caught between Byzantium and Persia; Lazica in the west
Georgia.summary: Kartli (Iberia), with its capital at Tiflis, was a Christian land whose nobles shifted between the two empires; in the later 580s they transferred their allegiance from Persia to Byzantium. The settlement of 591 divided Iberia roughly equally, with Persia keeping Tiflis. Laz and Iberian allies fought for Heraclius in 624, and in 627 he met the Western Turkish ruler outside Tiflis and besieged the city.

events.t: Khosrow II and Maurice divide Iberia, with Tiflis remaining on the Persian side.
Christian Caucasian allies, the Laz, Abasgians and Iberians, fight alongside Heraclius in Armenia.
Heraclius meets the Western Turkish ruler outside Tiflis, and their forces besiege the city.

Egypt.summary: Egypt's grain fed Constantinople and Byzantine armies. Its Coptic church was miaphysite and resisted the imperial Chalcedonian church. Persia invaded from 618–619, took Alexandria in June 619 and held Egypt until 629, pillaging monasteries. Amr ibn al-As later led the Arab Muslim conquest of Egypt.

events.t: Persian forces, invading from 618–619, take Alexandria (c. June 619) and soon control all Egypt.
Benjamin I becomes Coptic patriarch of Alexandria.
Persian troops withdraw from Alexandria (c. June 629), and Byzantine rule returns.

sources.title: Egypt iv. Relations in the Sasanian period
